sections.h2: What happens to a tenant when a North Carolina landlord sells the rental?
sections.html:
The tenant's deposit has to follow the sale. When a landlord's interest ends by sale, assignment, death or the appointment of a receiver, G.S. 42-54 gives the landlord 30 days to act.

The landlord either hands the remaining deposit to the new owner and mails the tenant notice of the transfer with the new owner's name and address, or returns the remaining deposit to the tenant. Either step relieves the seller of further liability for that money. A buyer who takes over tenants should get the deposit ledger, the leases and any written repair requests at closing.

sections.h2: How much security deposit can a North Carolina landlord hold?
sections.html:
The cap depends on the length of the tenancy. Under G.S. 42-51(b), a week-to-week tenancy allows two weeks' rent, a month-to-month tenancy allows one and one-half months' rent, and a term longer than month to month allows two months' rent.

  • Deposits may cover unpaid rent and certain water, sewer or electric charges.
  • They may cover damage to the unit, including damaged smoke or carbon monoxide alarms.
  • They may cover re-renting costs after a breach, including a broker's reasonable fee.
  • They may cover removal and storage of belongings after a summary ejectment case, plus court costs.

The landlord must account for the deposit in writing within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned. If the claim cannot be fixed by then, an interim accounting is due in 30 days and a final one within 60 days. Normal wear and tear cannot be charged, and the landlord cannot keep more than actual damages.

sections.h2: What repairs must a North Carolina landlord make?
sections.html:
The landlord must keep the home fit and habitable, and G.S. 42-42(a) spells out the duties. They include complying with building and housing codes, keeping common areas safe, and maintaining electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling systems, with prompt repair after the tenant gives written notice except in emergencies.

The statute also requires working smoke alarms, replaced or repaired within 15 days of the tenant's written notice, and at least one carbon monoxide alarm per rental unit per level in units with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage. Imminently dangerous conditions must be fixed within a reasonable time. The list includes unsafe wiring or steps, no potable water, no operable toilet and, from November 1 through March 31, no heating that can reach 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside.

A tenant cannot waive these duties by accepting a bad unit. For a seller, that means open code or alarm issues travel with the property, so ask your county inspections office what is on file.

sections.h2: Can a North Carolina landlord evict a tenant for asking for repairs?
sections.html:
No, not in retaliation. G.S. 42-37.1 protects good-faith repair requests, complaints to a government agency, a formal complaint by a government authority, efforts to enforce lease or legal rights, and joining a tenants' organization.

In a summary ejectment case, a tenant can raise retaliation as a defense by showing that the landlord's action substantially responds to one of those acts within 12 months before filing. The landlord can still prevail in several situations: the tenant breached the rent covenant or another substantial lease term, a fixed term ended without a renewal option, the tenant primarily caused the violation, code compliance requires emptying the unit, an earlier good-faith notice to quit was already delivered, or the owner in good faith wants the home as an abode, plans major remodeling, or will stop renting it for at least six months.

sections.h2: How much notice ends a North Carolina tenancy?
sections.html:
Source: G.S. 42-14, 42-3 and 42-26
SituationNotice or step
Year to yearOne month or more before the current year ends
Month to monthSeven days
Week to weekTwo days
Manufactured home space rentalAt least 60 days before the end of the rental period
Unpaid rentLease term forfeited if rent is not paid within 10 days after demand for all past-due rent

Summary ejectment under G.S. 42-26 covers holding over after the term, breaching a condition that ends the estate, and desertion while in arrears. Unpaid water, sewer or electric charges cannot be the basis for ending a lease.

sections.h2: How does a North Carolina eviction case move through court?
sections.html:
The landlord files in small claims before a magistrate, and hearings are set within 30 days of filing, usually within 10 to 15 days in eviction cases. The court system prints a $96 filing fee and a $30 sheriff service fee, and there is no jury in small claims.

  • A defendant served fewer than two days before the hearing is entitled to a continuance.
  • Either side can appeal to district court by noting appeal in court or in writing within 10 days of the decision.
  • Appeal costs must be paid, and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

A seller who wants a vacant house should plan around this timeline and should never change locks or remove belongings without a court order, since eviction in North Carolina runs through the court and the sheriff.

sections.h2: What happens to tenants when a North Carolina lender forecloses?
sections.html:
Tenants get a window, not an instant eviction. A notice of sale for residential property with fewer than 15 rental units must say that an order for possession may issue, and a tenant under a lease entered or renewed on or after October 1, 2007 may end it with at least 10 and no more than 90 days' notice after the sale date.

After a sale is reported, anyone can submit an upset bid within 10 days if it exceeds the last bid by at least 5% and at least $750, and each upset bid restarts a 10-day period. Until the sale is final, the owner of a rental can still try to sell the house privately, and a buyer who takes the rental subject to its leases will inherit the tenants' rights described above.

sections.h2: What should a seller of a North Carolina rental do before listing?
sections.html:
Start with the lease file. Confirm each tenant's term, the deposit amount and the date any notice to quit would run, then decide whether to sell with tenants in place or deliver vacant.

If tenants stay, give the buyer the deposit records so the 30-day transfer duty can be met. If the unit will be vacant, follow the notice periods and the court process, and do not rush a month-to-month tenant out with less than the seven-day notice the statute requires. Ask a North Carolina attorney to review the plan if a repair complaint is open, since a retaliation defense can slow a case.

faqs.q: How long does a North Carolina landlord have to return a security deposit?
faqs.a: The landlord must mail or deliver an itemized list of damage and the balance within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned. If the claim cannot be determined by then, an interim accounting is due in 30 days and a final one within 60 days.

faqs.q: What is the maximum security deposit in North Carolina?
faqs.a: It is two weeks' rent for week-to-week tenancies, one and one-half months' rent for month-to-month, and two months' rent for longer terms.

faqs.q: How many days notice does a month-to-month tenant get in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Seven days. Week-to-week tenancies need two days, and year-to-year tenancies need one month or more before the year ends.

faqs.q: What happens to the deposit when a North Carolina landlord sells?
faqs.a: The landlord must within 30 days either transfer the remaining deposit to the new owner and notify the tenant by mail, or return the remaining deposit to the tenant.

faqs.q: Can a North Carolina tenant stay after a foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: For a while. The notice of sale for small residential rentals must say an order for possession may issue, and tenants under qualifying leases may end the lease on 10 to 90 days' notice after the sale date.
